name: Fatima Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, and the first thing is the cattle. We run about ninety suckler cows, that means cows that raise their own calves for beef, on the farm at Hollow Bridge, with a few fields of barley for feed and the rest in hay. My partner Ravi drives for the dairy co-op, so most days it's me and our neighbour's lad, Jonah, two mornings a week. I love calving when it goes right, and I hate chasing the hay weather, checking the forecast four times a day in June.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new tools in your work now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I asked one of the chat programs to help me write a grant application for new fencing last spring, and it was decent once I'd fixed the bits it got wrong about our soil. Ravi's sister showed me, I'd never have tried it on my own. I don't let it near the cattle records, those are on the government system anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for the paperwork and leave it there. I'd tell the women's farming group it saved me an evening on that grant. If someone on the forum was panicking, I'd say calm down, it can't tell a heifer's in trouble from the way she's standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a small win for me. The bit of farming I hate is the forms, and if that gets quicker I get more evenings with the kids. It doesn't touch what pays the bills, which is weight on the cattle and the price at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it a bit more for the paperwork, the subsidy claims and the bank letters, once I'd seen Ravi's sister do hers. I'd still buy the new cattle crush, the metal pen we hold them in for the vet, about four thousand, which I'd been saving for. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit pleased, honestly, at the idea of fewer forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it got things wrong about your soil. Did that put you off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, at first. It said our land was good for growing wheat, and anyone who's walked my fields after rain knows it's heavy clay that sticks to your boots. So now I check everything it writes, like I'd check a new farm hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, help Mira with her maths homework, because I'm usually doing it half-asleep at the kitchen table. And maybe go to the pub quiz with Ravi once a month. Small things.

S0.say: It's useful for the paperwork, and I'd leave it there. It saved me an evening on a grant, but it can't tell when a heifer is in trouble from the way she stands.
S0.think: It's a small win, because the forms are the part of farming I hate most. It doesn't touch what pays the bills, which is weight on the cattle and the market price.
S0.do: Uses AI a little more for subsidy claims and bank letters, after seeing a relative do it first. Buys the cattle crush she'd saved for, about four thousand, and changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit pleased at the idea of fewer forms.
S0.quote: Anyone who's walked my fields after rain knows it's heavy clay that sticks to your boots. So now I check everything it writes, like I'd check a new farm hand.
S0.fieldNote: She treats the tool like a new worker on trial, which captures her steady style well. She only tried it because a relative showed her first. The gain she pictures is time with her daughter, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if companies are cutting beginner jobs, they should pay into apprenticeships, and the government should make them. I'd say it in the group chat and at the union branch meeting. Young people need a first rung on the ladder, and it's not fair to pull it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow is fine, I've got time to watch what other farmers try. The bit that bothers me is Jonah. He's nineteen and he's hoping to get a job at the feed merchants, and that's exactly the kind of place that might hire fewer beginners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer Jonah three days a week instead of two, if the numbers work, maybe an extra hundred and twenty a week. I'd keep using the chat program for forms and maybe try one of the herd apps the vet keeps mentioning, once a couple of neighbours have it. And I'd keep the savings where they are, about three months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady for me, but protective of Jonah. Like watching a calf go out into a field with a bull in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you afford the extra day for Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only just. It'd mean not replacing the old quad bike for another year and patching the tyres instead. But I'd rather do that than watch him go off to a warehouse in the city where nobody knows his name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which neighbour would you watch first with the herd app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete Morgan up the hill. He's always first with gadgets and he's always honest about which ones were rubbish. If Pete says it found a sick cow two days early, I'd buy it.

S1.say: If companies cut beginner jobs, they should pay into apprenticeships, and the government should make them. Young people need a first rung on the ladder.
S1.think: A slow change suits me, because I can watch what other farmers try first. What bothers me is Jonah, who is nineteen and hoping for a beginner's job at the feed merchants.
S1.do: Offers Jonah a third day a week, about an extra hundred and twenty, and puts off replacing the quad bike to pay for it. Tries a herd app once a neighbour has proven it, and keeps her three months of savings untouched.
S1.feel: Steady for herself but protective of the young farm hand.
S1.quote: Like watching a calf go out into a field with a bull in it.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry went straight to the young man who works for her, not to herself. She'd pay for his extra day with her own small sacrifice, the quad bike. Her rule for new tools is clear: wait for Pete up the hill to try it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a voice in this, and the unions should be fighting for retraining money, not just shouting. I'd post that the government should make the companies pay for it. I'd also say, gently, that the people at the market and the abattoir still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Ravi worries me a bit. He drives for the co-op, but half his day is the delivery app and the office telling him routes, and if the office goes automatic, who knows what they do next. Mostly though, I think it's the buyers I'd watch, because the big meat processors would use it to bid us down even harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the beef producers' group properly, pay the fee, about two hundred a year, because if prices get pushed we need to push back together. I'd start selling a few boxes of beef direct to families in town, maybe ten animals' worth, using the chat program to set up the order page. And I'd make sure Ravi's got his heavy goods licence renewed early, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be doing things, not sitting worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the processors bid you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are only three that matter round here, and they already set the price on a Monday and we take it. If a computer is working out exactly how little we'll accept, it'll find that number. That's not the AI's fault, it's that there are too few buyers, and nobody in government does anything about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the chat program for the beef boxes. Isn't that the same technology you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yes, fair. It's a tool, like a hammer. It's who holds the hammer and how hard they swing it that bothers me.

S2.say: Workers need a voice, and the unions should fight for retraining money paid for by the companies. And the market and the abattoir still need farmers.
S2.think: My partner Ravi's driving job is run by an office that might go automatic, and that worries me. Mostly though, I'd watch the big meat processors using it to bid us down.
S2.do: Joins the beef producers' group for about two hundred a year and starts selling around ten animals' worth of beef boxes direct to families, using a chat program for the order page. Gets Ravi's heavy goods licence renewed early.
S2.feel: Anxious, but in a busy, practical way.
S2.quote: It's a tool, like a hammer. It's who holds the hammer and how hard they swing it that bothers me.
S2.fieldNote: When I pointed out she'd use the same technology she was wary of, she laughed and gave the hammer line without missing a beat. Her real target is the small number of meat buyers, not AI as such. She turns worry into tasks almost instantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if share prices are booming while people lose their jobs, then those gains have to be taxed and shared. I'd go on the march if there was one. I'd also be careful what I said at the market, because half the people there vote the other way and I've still got to sell to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, beef might be fine for a bit. People still eat. But if lots of office people lose jobs, they'll buy mince, not steak, and my beef boxes won't sell. And Mira wants to be a vet, and if AI matches skilled professionals, I'd wonder what part of that job is left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch the beef boxes toward cheaper cuts and family packs. I'd sit down with Mira, she's thirteen, and talk honestly about the hands-on side of vet work, the calvings and the surgery, because that's the bit that stays. And I'd ask the bank about fixing the mortgage, because with house prices booming I'd expect rates to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for the farm today, but for the kind of world my kids grow up in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her, the computer might read the X-ray, love, but it can't get its arm inside a cow at two in the morning. She'd pull a face, she always does when I mention that. But she'd remember it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch what you say at the market. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because farming is a small world and people have long memories. I'd rather argue for a fairer tax quietly through the union than lose a customer over it. That's not cowardly, it's just how you survive round here.

S3.say: If share prices boom while people lose jobs, those gains have to be taxed and shared. I'd march, but I'd watch what I said at the market.
S3.think: People still eat, so beef might be fine for a while, but out-of-work office staff buy mince, not steak. I'd also wonder what's left of the vet job my daughter Mira wants.
S3.do: Moves the beef boxes toward cheaper cuts and family packs. Talks with thirteen-year-old Mira about the hands-on side of vet work, and asks the bank about fixing the mortgage before rates jump.
S3.feel: Uneasy, less about the farm today than about the world her children will grow up in.
S3.quote: The computer might read the X-ray, love, but it can't get its arm inside a cow at two in the morning.
S3.fieldNote: There was a clear gap between her public politics and what she'd say at the market, and she defended it as survival, not cowardice. Her thinking runs through customers' wallets to her prices. The daughter's ambition to be a vet brought the scenario home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms need rules, safety checks and a fair deal for the workers they replace, and I'd say it loudly. I'd be on the union's side and I'd write to our representative. I'd also say plainly that some robot jobs on a farm would be welcome, like lifting bales, if the people aren't just thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the hay is gone to the robots first, the baling and stacking, and that's half my year. The cattle, I'm less sure, a robot can feed them but I don't know about calving. The big ranches would get them first and their beef would be cheaper than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the farm show and see the robots for real before I believed any of it. I'd ask Pete what he's buying. If they could be rented through the machinery ring, the group of farms that share kit, I'd rent one for hay and keep the money for the cattle. I'd also push the beef boxes harder, because local and grass-fed is what the robots can't sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not beaten. It's like a bad spring, you get through it but you lose some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Jonah in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me up. If the robot bales the hay, there's no third day for Jonah, maybe no second day. I'd try to keep him on the cattle, but I'd be lying if I said I could promise it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd rent a robot. Doesn't that go against the union side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does a bit, yes, and I don't love it. But if I don't, I go under and nobody gets a job here. I'd rather be the farm that kept Jonah on two days with a robot than the farm that sold up to a company with ten robots and no Jonahs.

S4.say: Robots on farms need rules, safety checks and a fair deal for the workers they replace. Some robot jobs, like lifting bales, would be welcome if people aren't just thrown out.
S4.think: The hay goes to robots first, and that's half my year. Big ranches would get them first, and their beef would be cheaper than mine.
S4.do: Goes to the farm show to see the robots for real and asks Pete what he's buying. Rents a hay robot through the machinery ring if possible, and pushes the local, grass-fed beef boxes harder.
S4.feel: Alarmed but not beaten, like getting through a bad spring and losing some along the way.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the farm that kept Jonah on two days with a robot than the farm that sold up to a company with ten robots and no Jonahs.
S4.fieldNote: This was the hardest moment: her union instincts against her plan to rent a robot. She owned the tension rather than hiding it. Jonah, the nineteen-year-old helper, is the person through whom she feels every scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because it goes after the hay and then the people like Jonah. What would help is a machinery ring that rents robots cheaply to small farms, so it's not only the big ranches who get them. And rules so a farm worker who loses hours gets paid training, properly, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's selling the robots and who's buying the beef. It's the same few big names, I'd bet, at both ends. That's what I'd want someone to look into.

headlineQuote: The computer might read the X-ray, love, but it can't get its arm inside a cow at two in the morning.
portrait: Fatima is a 43-year-old beef farmer at Hollow Bridge with about ninety suckler cows and fields of hay, living with her partner Ravi, a co-op driver, and two children. She's union-minded and wants companies to pay for retraining, but she's practical and uses AI for forms once someone she trusts has tried it first. She moves through the scenarios by turning worry into tasks: more days for her young helper Jonah, beef boxes sold direct, a renewed driving licence for Ravi. In the robot scenario she'd rent a machine through a shared ring and admits that clashes with her union instincts.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because robots would take the hay work first and then the hours of helpers like Jonah.
whatWouldHelp: A machinery ring that rents robots cheaply to small farms, and paid training for farm workers who lose hours.
